analysis.one_liner: Ends all federal funding and benefits under the Affordable Care Act.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 32 Senate Republicans, was placed on the Senate calendar in July 2013 and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would prohibit any federal money from being spent to carry out the Affordable Care Act — including premium subsidies, Medicaid expansion payments to states, and marketplace operations. It would end every entitlement to benefits under the law and rescind any unspent funds. It was read twice and placed on the Senate calendar, and the Senate never took it up before the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main gainers would have been people and employers opposed to the ACA's requirements, since the law's spending, benefit obligations, and state payments would all stop. The federal Treasury would keep the unobligated balances and stop making ACA payments in the short term. Note that the bill bans spending but does not repeal the law's taxes, so revenue would continue to flow in while benefits end.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any federal funds from being used to carry out the Affordable Care Act or the health provisions of the 2010 reconciliation act.
Ends all entitlements to benefits under the ACA on the date of enactment, so no further benefit payments could be made.
Prohibits any payments from being awarded, owed, or made to any state, district, or territory under the ACA, cutting off federal money for measures like the Medicaid expansion.
Rescinds all unobligated balances available under the ACA, pulling back money already appropriated but not yet spent.

analysis.who_pays: Low- and middle-income households would bear the cost: people receiving premium subsidies to buy coverage, states and beneficiaries in the Medicaid expansion, and people with preexisting conditions who gained access under the law. Insurers and hospitals would also lose the subsidized customer base and reduced uncompensated care that came with the law's funding.
analysis.who_pays_short: People relying on ACA coverage help

drawbacks.text: The bill would end premium subsidies, Medicaid expansion payments to states, and all benefit entitlements under the ACA, taking coverage help away from the low- and middle-income people it serves.

It prohibits spending on the ACA without repealing the law's revenue provisions, so taxes collected under the law would continue while every dollar raised is barred from paying for the law's benefits — a half-repeal that collects money and spends nothing.
Rescinding unobligated balances would pull back funds already appropriated, including money states and programs were counting on receiving.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Whatever the Treasury saved in the short run would come entirely from taking health coverage help away from ordinary people, and the bill was poorly designed even on its own terms: it defunds the law without repealing its taxes, leaving money flowing in that can no longer be spent on benefits.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in July 2013, read twice, and placed on the Senate's calendar, and the Democratic majority never brought it up for a vote before the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Sen. Ted Cruz introduced the bill on July 11, 2013, with 25 senators joining as original cosponsors in the introduction.
A total of 32 senators, all Republicans, cosponsored the bill.
On July 16, 2013, the bill was read a second time and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 135) — a holding spot on the Senate's business list.
No further action was ever recorded; the bill never received a vote or a hearing, and the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 with the bill still sitting on the calendar.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people came out ahead: because the bill never moved, ACA premium subsidies, Medicaid expansion payments, and benefit entitlements stayed funded. Health insurers and hospitals also kept the subsidized customers and reduced uncompensated care that depend on that funding.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People whose ACA coverage stayed funded

for.name: Sen. Ted Cruz
for.role: U.S. Senator from Texas; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Defund Obamacare Act of 2013 to prohibit all federal funding and benefits under the ACA.

for.name: 32 of 45 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it the support of most of the Senate Republican conference.

against.name: Sen. Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill up for a vote; it sat on the Senate calendar until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 32 cosponsors were Republicans, and the Democratic majority never scheduled the bill for a vote.

industries.note: Defunding the ACA would end the premium subsidies that brought insurers millions of new customers — the same money ordinary people use to afford coverage, so the industry's interest in stopping this bill ran alongside the public's.

The bill cuts off federal payments under the ACA, including Medicaid expansion money; providers backed that funding because it reduced unpaid care, and losing it would push those costs back onto patients and hospitals alike.
The bill prohibits any ACA payments to states, ending the federal money states were receiving to run the Medicaid expansion and other programs.
